source.title: Latent Action Pretraining from Videos
source.authors: Seonghyeon Ye; Joel Jang; Byeongguk Jeon; Se June Joo; Jianwei Yang; Baolin Peng; A. Mandlekar; Reuben Tan; Yu-Wei Chao; Bill Yuchen Lin; Lars Lidén; Kimin Lee; Jian-Feng Gao; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Dieter Fox; Minjoon Seo

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream-task outcomes while varying model and data scale, but it does not measure held-out language-model cross-entropy or fit the claimed loss laws.
record.gate_note: The paper uses scaling laws as motivation and reports scaling ablations for LAPA. It does not measure pretraining loss, test power-law fits or extrapolation, compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or test architectural-shape effects. The rows cover only reported downstream-performance scaling results; values available only in plots are marked figure only.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation for small scaling ablations of a robot VLA pipeline. It varies the size of the latent action quantizer (30–300M), not the 7B policy. Its pretraining data are robot or human video, and its measure is downstream robot-task success rate. It reports no held-out loss, fits no power law, and makes no predictions across scale. Four rising points do not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss, and the system is not a language model. The authors say they leave exploring scaling laws to future work. The ablations are a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say scaling the quantizer model, the data and the latent action space benefits LAPA, and that the optimal latent-action-space scale depends on action complexity. They explicitly leave exploring scaling laws for human video to future work, citing compute cost. Their claim that full human-video data improves all subtasks is contradicted by Spoon2Towel in Table 12.
record.recipe_differences: Uses robot manipulation success rates rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy; varies LAPA model/data scales rather than fitting loss laws or compute-optimal parameter/token splits.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors say the optimal latent-action-space scale depends on action complexity; increasing sequence length is less effective than increasing vocabulary size for Language Table.

fits_no_version.finding: For a robot VLA (LAPA), downstream SIMPLER success rises modestly as the latent action quantizer grows from 30M to 300M and as the Bridgev2 fraction grows (Fig. 5a-b). Human-video data scaling from 10% to full Sthv2 gives mixed per-task results (Table 12): the average moves 50.0 to 52.1 and one task falls 66.6 to 50.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream success of latent-action robot policies improves with the size of the action tokenizer and of the pretraining video data.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is downstream robot-task success, not language-model loss. Some scaling results are only shown in figures, with no exact values stated in the text; the human-video data-scaling results vary by task, and the reported table provides no uncertainty for those comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: Latent-action sequence-length and vocabulary-size ablations (Figure 5c-d and Figure 16), window-size tests (Figure 15a), and qualitative latent-action analyses were not included because they do not measure model/data scaling outcomes named by V6.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No comparison of shape at fixed parameter count.
Uses video pretraining but fits no power-law form in any regime.
No language-model downstream tasks. No predictive relation with scale or loss; only a few-point robot-success ablation on the quantizer and data size.
No fitted exponents and no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification is wrong. The scaled component is a 30–300M tokenizer, the policy stays fixed at 7B, and the measure is robot success with 24 rollouts per task. Most differences are a few rollouts, and no uncertainty is reported for the scaling ablations. Nothing here bears on language-model scaling laws as stated in V1–V7.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and tokens.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although the study uses video pretraining, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds for video or other training regimes.
The study measures downstream robot-task success under selected model/data scaling changes, not held-out pretraining loss or a quantitative predictive relationship.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices, and no test for curves bending away from a power law.
